Ключевые авторы Hero-U, Кори и Лори Коул, в 1980-х — 1990-х работали в Sierra над играми серии Quest for Glory. И если амбиции той же серии King's Quest в основном ограничивались передовыми для своего времени графикой и звуком, то Quest for Glory замахивалась в другую сторону: что, если взять стандартный Sierra'вский движок для адвенчур и сделать на нем RPG?

Эту справку я сейчас толкнул не для того, чтобы сказать, получился ли из Hero-U иденый продолжатель Quest for Glory или нет. Это для того, чтобы сказать: с этой игрой авторы тоже решили взять привычные рамки жанра и растянуть их до невозможности. У тебя в игре, которая по всем признакам напоминает классический квест, появляются position-based боёвка, ход времени, побочные квесты, мир игры, выстроенный далеко за пределами сюжета, ДЕЙТИНГ. В итоге вроде бы включил классический квест, а играешь в Persona с духом вселенной Гарри Поттера.

Возможно, игра закусилась на нечто большее, чем могли вытянуть разработчики. Я сейчас, насколько я понимаю, не дошел и до половины внутриигрового времени. При этом я одновременно и упустил ряд побочных возможностей, и успел забыть, что я вообще тут по сюжету должен делать и зачем. Кажется, игре пошло бы на пользу, если бы она была более сжатой и динамичной, а также если бы она активно помогала игроку перепроходить упущенные дни. Bomber's Notebook из TLoZ: Majora's Mask или система сохранений из Papers Please — вот такого бы сюда.

Кажется, что игре, которая наводит игрока на вопрос "а зачем это всё?", нельзя ставить хорошую оценку. И всё-таки — рекомендую. Это очень авторская игра, и чувствуется, что люди, несколько выпавшие из современного течения отрасли, от всей души и считай ручным трудом попытались сделать в хорошем смысле БОЛЬШУЮ игру.

I thoroughly enjoyed the storyline, lore, references to previous quest for glory games, and general play style. The mini-games were fun and I think the game would have benefited from including more of them (darts, pool, etc.) rather than just having them as screenshots/cutscenes. 

My main complaint was the gameplay itself which was simultaneously too much and too little. There was lots to interact with in the environment but very little of it was meaningful or useful. IMO, point and click games should be a bit more restrictive in terms of what can be interacted with to drive the player towards what is needed to complete the story. When there are literally dozens of clickable objects (with multiple options on what to do with them) on a single page, anything truly important is drowned out in all of the other noise and it becomes a chore to click through them all and find what is relevant. I get the concept of red herrings and not making the story too linear but come on...

[spoiler] For example, as far as I could tell, just about every lighting device (sconce, torch, candle, etc.) was clickable yet at no point was it ever helpful to click on them. For the first several hours of gameplay I thought there MUST be a secret passageway or something hidden at some point to justify having them all clickable in the game so I continued to check through them individually but nothing ever materialized. [/spoiler]

One other minor issue was the rather bizarre romance options. Several felt forced or unnecessary and a few options that felt like they should have been viable, weren't. Nothing game-breaking but unnecessarily frustrating at times.

Overall, a lot of the game (read: unnecessary clickable objects) could have been cut out without sacrificing anything of note which would have made for a more pleasant overall experience. That being said, the game was still fun and if you've got a nostalgia itch for the quest for glory games this should scratch it.

Worthy successor to the Quest for Glory series.
It's a shame Point and Click RPGs died with QfG because this game proves it they can still be done well and be very entertaining. In terms of story, character interactions, puns and just sheer content this game towers over it's predecessors.
Still, I had couple of gripes. One of them is while Quest for Glory had a lot of replayability due to different solutions to problems depending on class and skill choice, in this game you are rogue and there is not that much you can do about it, you'll be raising pretty much every single stat you have and because of that there is little reason to replay the game, since you most likely gonna end up doing things mostly the same.
Tied to this fact are the puzzles. Like in Quest for Glory puzzle solutions are tied to be being trained in a specific skill rather than monkey wrench logic, but because you are supposed to be trained in every skill the alternative puzzle solutions are rather rare and usually insignificant.
Other minor gripe I had is that the game offers certain task to complete that don't really have any tangible rewards on their own. I get it - it's roleplaying game so often you'll help someone just because you felt like it or because that's a type of character you are playing but from gameplay perspective it just left me scratching my head wondering if I did something wrong or out of order because game didn't react at all to any information I gathered or situation I resolved by doing it.
Still, game is absolutely worth it's asking price, and as a fan of original Quest for Glory series I had a blast playing through it. Hopefully we can expect a sequel or another game of this genre soon.

Succeeds in being a spiritual successor to Quest for Gory, albeit more RPG based than Point & Click puzzles. You are also limited to being a Thief, but plenty of choices in how you deal with situations. The day/night curfew may be stressful at first, but once you relax and go with the flow it becomes less of an issue.

It gets boring closer to the end, but being a Quest For Glory fan, there's only one question that could be asked: "So you want to be a Hero?"
And yeah, black bird is back!

I think it's my fault for going into this, hoping for a spiritual successor to the wonderful Quest for Glory series, which I absolutely adored, but this game was a huge disappointment for me. It's too restrictive to be fun, and the strict timings you have to adhere to means there's not a lot of freedom to explore and do as you wish.

If you were a fan of the [b]Quest For Glory[/b] (and other point-and-click adventure) games of the 90's, then you'll probably feel right at home with Hero-U.

[h2]The Good[/h2]
This feels like it's made by people who love good stories, and love to immerse others in them. The characters, dialog, locations, atmosphere, and overall storytelling contribute to an engaging experience that pulled me in like a book I didn't want to put down. It doesn't take itself too seriously, weaving heartfelt narrative themes with threads of lighthearted banter, cheesy rhymes conscious of their own cheesiness, and a peppering of dad jokes. I find this nuanced balanced increasingly rare in books, not to mention in games, so I was quite tickled to encounter this gem. 

Visually, I appreciated the lo-fi, semi-pixelated look of most of the game, which gave it a retro, nostalgic feel. A lot of care and talent went into the design and artwork, much of which is meticulously hand-drawn. The locations and maps don't have that random, procedurally-generated feel, but seem carefully curated and planned.

The music completes the storytelling. It's never too epic for the encounter or too whimsical for the occasion. I don't know whether the score was written by multiple talents, or a single... either way it's always 'just right'. Dynamic enough to engross, but tasteful so as not to distract.

[h2]The Bad[/h2]
The game lacks some of the polish and production value of the original QFG/Sierra games . I found the hi-res, 3D-modeled player, NPCs, and other random 3D elements to be out of place with the rest of the pixel-rich artwork. The overall visual experience felt a bit disjointed.

In the end, these are minor (and arguably tedious) considerations, but worth noting. 

[h2]Worth It?[/h2]
Absolutely.

All in all, Hero-U is a fun throwback that I enjoyed playing and would love to see a sequel to.

Developed by the same people who made the Quest for Glory series, this is a good spiritual successor. I like the game's writing and there are a lot of interesting characters. The setting is fun too. The game has some of that Kickstarter jank, but it doesn't really get in the way of enjoying the game. There is some backer designed content, but thankfully its not intrusive and or terrible like certain other games. The game is clearly designed to be part of a series, but it has a satisfying conclusion and it doesn't feel like you need to buy the sequels to get a complete and satisfying experience.

There is one major issue with the game. I do not like how the game has a time limit. I feel like the game handles time limits very poorly. It barely ever gives any indication when a deadline to finish an event is. It also gives the players hints about how to do something well before they actually can use the hint because its time-locked. This often leads to situations where the player can wonder if they are missing something they need to do or if they just need to wait. Its also hard to tell what stats to focus on. This can lead the player to make a single bad choice, and leave themselves at a significant disadvantage. Magic is worthless, and the player can miss out on learning the two other skills which are actually useful. 

Now some people might argue that since the Quest for Glory games had a time limit mechanic, Rogue U should too. I disagree. A game shouldn't keep an unfun and annoying mechanic just because the prior games had it.  I also understand that the time limit is there to prevent players from just grinding stats and getting bored, but I believe if someone wants to grind, the game should let them. 

Overall, though I enjoyed the game, and I hope this is just the start of a new game franchise.

This is part Adventure, part RPG, part time-management. The story is basically 100% linear across the 50-day school session. All objectives are optional, but you need to pass a certain bar to get the best ending. You altogether have quite a lot of time to do the time-limited tasks, so even with somewhat inefficient play, if you are making an honest effort, you'll probably be okay. The major quests give you good clues, so there's no "moon logic" here.

There are tons of conversation trees and random objects to play with, filled with mostly-clever and humorous commentary from Shawn (the player character). It's a game just as much about trying every single random thing to see what Shawn will say.

There are a couple of mutually exclusive paths and sidequests that are difficult to find, especially on a first play. So it can be nice to play a second time (or come back and play a third time after a long while).

The worst part of the game is that the skill training is a bit grindy. You can generally only learn 5 points of a skill (out of 100) each game day. And then, once you do learn how to manage your days efficiently, you have way more time than you need and it's a pain to keep clicking Shawn's bed to sleep through the excess one in-game hour at a time. However, there are lots of games that are a bit repetitive in a calm way (Harvest Moon, zero-plot simulator games, etc.), so I'm sure some players see this as a positive.

Second worst thing is that some of the dialogue can be pretty stupid. It's kind of spread throughout in random places, but less than 5% altogether. And then there's pretty much zero point to having any conversation with Sophia the receptionist. All she does is call Shawn a series of stupid and inappropriate pet names from first to last meeting while being generally whiny about nonsense and giving you no helpful information.

Overall I still give a generally positive rating, and better if you can get a 50% off sale.

I'm giving the game a positive review even though it is highly flawed. I had a lot of fun playing it, and I was able to do most of the different things there are to do, and explored all the areas, both common and hidden. The beginning of the game was great, the middle got boring, and the ending was excellent. I felt very accomplished by being able to defeat bosses and situations by a combination of combat and diplomacy, but I was very disappointed I did not win the game by achieving Rogue of the Year.

The reasons I didn't like it were the constant restrictiveness of the clock. You had to be done exploring for dinnertime and bedtime, and if you weren't you got teleported out of your current place to the dining room or bedroom. I achieved finishing an advanced elective course, but that meant I had to be at the classroom by 3pm every day. Another thing that was very annoying was how things unfolded at certain days.

I ended up not achieving Rogue of the Year because a fellow classmate died, and I couldn't rescue him because he died in the catacombs, which at that point I had not yet unlocked. I played it all the way through, only using a save-game once to back-track, but if you want to do everything and win you'd be hard pressed to do it without a walkthrough. Overall, it was a fun ride.

First things first. If you’re pinning for the Quest for Glories series, I suggest you start with [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/sinocelt/recommended/283880/][i]Heroine’s Quest: The Herald of Ragnarok[/i][/url].

Now to [i]Hero-U[/i]. This game is great in some ways and really bad in others.

Great are the sense of wonder and adventure, the many tales you can weave yourself into, and the varied places you can discover. In these respects—as in the humor—[i]Hero-U[/i] is a proud heir to [url= https://store.steampowered.com/app/502750/Quest_for_Glory_15/]the Quest for Glory series[/url].

The graphics are good, overall. A lot of places do elicit wonder, as do some of the 2D drawings. Many other 2D drawings, however, are … less inspired. Also, the 2D and 3D renditions of the same characters differ noticeably.

The characters themselves are … OK? Honestly, I don’t know why they didn’t engage me more than they did. They have interesting personalities and backstories, and even their own side quests for some.

The fights are slow and boring. And numerous. You can try to sneak around them (though not if you want to become able to help some of the characters with their side quests), but sneaking is itself very slow. And if you get caught, you have to fight, and if you’ve avoided fighting up to then, you aren’t gonna win.

[i]Hero-U[/i] is very grindy. Sure, there was some grind in Quest for Glory, but here the game is longer and the grind exponentially worse. It sucked out any pleasure I had in playing, after a while.

This game doesn’t even [i]need[/i] the grind. The grind is something other games use to inflate themselves artificially, but [i]Hero-U[/i] would be a long game even without it. So I wish the grind had been reduced somehow. Or replaced by another system altogether, even if that distanced [i]Hero-U[/i] from Quest for Glory.

One aspect of Quest for Glory that [i]Hero-U[/i] didn’t replicate, alas, is the variety of ways to tackle the same situation. In Quest for Glory, many puzzles could be solved differently by the three character classes (four, if you count the Paladin). Not so here, since there’s only one character class: rogue. The magic, as a result, had very limited utility out of combat. No [i]fetch[/i] spell. No [i]open[/i] spell. No [i]levitate[/i] spell. <sob>

Finally, the ending was a letdown. Some of the side quests (notably Katie’s) were a lot more exciting, and had a much more thrilling climaxes, than the main arc did.

This game is fun to play, with an immersive world, great music and exciting non-player characters to interact with.  The art is gorgeous, the story and world-building are very interesting.  If you're also a fan of the Quest for Glory series, this is a worthy and wonderful successor to that set of games, and so has a lot of nostalgia value.  But if you've never played those games, this one stands on its own as something very exciting to play.  It may even pique your curiosity to try out those older games!  I love this. [h1][b][u]BottomLine at the Top:[/u][/b][/h1] 
This is another example of a game that made me wish Steam had a neutral option for rating games.  Ultimately though I have to say that this ended up feeling like a chore to finish.  


[h1][b][u]Intro:[/u][/b][/h1]
I went into this title strongly biased. Growing up on the QFQ series I was immediately intrigued when I saw that Lori and Cory Cole had started their own studio and developed a new title in the vein of the QFG series.  


[h1][b][u]Pros:[/u][/b][/h1]

-Probably the one thing that stuck out the most in this game was the level of object interaction.  Nearly everything on the screen is clickable and interactable with I'd say at least 95% having unique interactions, descriptions and writing for each.  This is an extremely tedious process and I give made probs for the development team for this work.  
-I think the setup for the story and character design are mostly fairly good.  I’ll get into why it doesn't really work out in the long run though shortly.


[h1][b][u]Meh...:[/u][/b][/h1]

-Annoying to go back and forth between the character stat screen and equipment selection screen to see what effect each item has on stats. 
-Updating equipment doesn't change character style.  This is keeping in line with QFG and other RPG type games, but here it sticks out for some reason.   
-Main menu style underwhelming.
-Intro video is low resolution, choppy
-No voice work.  Again, this can and has worked in many P&C games.  In this case I am unsure if it’s really a negative as I think all of the puns would have gotten old quickly.  I also think it would have upped the cost of the game substantially due to all the unique interactions and dialogue.  
-Music is decent but gets repetitive.  
-The overall interface and game design makes me think they might have been attempting to make a title compatible with mobile OS’s.  I would almost think this is comparable to one of those cheapo mass produced mobile OS RPG games were it not for the somewhat better story and writing then you’d find in one of those.  


[h1][b][u]Cons:[/u][/b][/h1]

-For those looking for a quest for glory reboot, this is not it.  
-There are no character classes (closest is you get to choose two of three "Electives").  
-You are essentially locked in the school so there is no sense of world exploration like in QFG.  
-The RPG elements are underwhelming, and character building takes FOREVER with little pay off.  
-Fights are boring and repetitive.  Often goes to overhead view which is ugly.  Had one or two occasions where there were clipping errors due to view change.
-So much of this game feels tedious.  The time mechanic makes it really feel like I’m at a school. Go to class, do one or two stat building activities, go to elective, eat dinner, do an additional thing, repeat.  Repeat...REPEAT....ughhh.  
-No direct inventory interaction (i.e. dragging objects out of inventory to use on environment/other objects).  In some P&C’s this can work but, in this case, it really just adds to the lack of immersion and overall sense of tedium. You can literally do all your interactions by pressing the 1-5 keys on your keyboard.  
-Ughhhhhh....here’s a good one: The triggering for being able to proceed with certain events and actions is a pain.  The game will hint that you need to perform a certain action (like finding a hidden door).  You quickly find where the door most likely is, but you can't choose to open it UNTIL a specific day.  This makes you waste time on things trying to do things you can't actually do yet.  
-The poobah card game is dumb.  I had to continually reference a reddit post about how to play.  It takes too long, and you can't set your own bet amount. Also, the availability of the game starts early on, but I didn't have enough money to play until many game days later.  
-The dating mechanic is, again, tedious and feels like something that might have been an interesting idea but just didn’t pan out here.
-EXTREMELY UNDERWHELMING ENDING.  


[h1][b][u]Final Thoughts:[/u][/b][/h1] 
I really hate to say this, but I was glad when I was finally done with this game.  The ending would have actually made me upset if I wasn't so relieved it was finally over.  Halfway through I had already invested 10+ hours of time and I wanted to see it through so I could write a comprehensive review.  It appears Transolar Games is doubling down on this world they've built here; I see they already have a similar game styled more towards a younger crowd in the same game world and there are many references to a future sequel(s).  I do not believe I will be checking any of those out.  Still, the Cole's are legendary P&C designers, so I am really hoping that they shift to a more faithful QFG style adaptation in the future and wish them the best of luck.  

I did not pay full price for this game and could not possibly recommend anyone else to do the same.

Hero U is a lovingly crafted and respectful successor to the old Sierra 'Quest for Glory' games. This will make it nostalgia fuel for some, but leave some of the references 'over the heads' of non QFG fans.
If you have never played a QFG game, this is a cute title about going to a school for heroes, where you grind up your stats in a day-to-day time management game. Your days are spent going to class, training skills, and making friends/enemies.
The game contains combat, equipment, magic/alchemical items, and differing dungeons with some different enemies to explore.
You read stories, ask questions and take tests while trying to avoid getting demerits and being kicked out of school.

The good;
-For QFG fans, this is a game set in that world, with lots of respectfully made references back to those great games of old.
-The story and character are interesting and diverse. I wish there was greater emphasis placed on the different characters, their individual goals, and generally more/deeper interactions with them.
-The various events that pop up throughout the games 50 odd days, add interesting problems, unique situations, and enjoyable obstacles for the player to overcome.
-The unique events that come up throughout the story are a fun diversion with puzzles and interesting content. I wish there were more of these.

The Bad;
-Most of the content is fairly shallow; 
Problem -> solution -> resolution, without much impact beyond a few comments, this describes most of the game. Outside of one or two points that I won't spoil, your decisions don't have much meaningful impact. While exploration is fun, I had quickly managed to fully explore the new areas as they unlocked. Most of which had little impact once their event was over.
-The grind gets very repetitive very quickly;
 I found myself getting bored with the same 'grind stat until dinner', while this is broken a little by the unique events, there are not nearly enough of them to completely mask the wash, rinse, repeat. Simply put, the cycle of ‘go-to A get apple’ ‘go to B give apple’ ‘get “X liked that” ‘…. Gets boring by the third time I did it, let alone the thirtyish… 
-The constant need to revisit locations and make sure you don't miss anything is just a disappointing and aggravating time sink;
Many of the game's intrigues and secondary plot points, don't come up unless you visit certain areas on certain days (sometimes at specific times). As there is no real indicator of this, I found myself constantly treading over the same ground, day after day, to make sure that I found all the possible events. For example, there is a character that appears in a specific room, but not every night. Learning their story requires you to enter that room on several of these nights. As I did not know which nights this character was present, I ended up repeatedly visiting this room every night (usually by saving first, sneaking there, and loading my saved game if they were not present).
- The lack of a real ending just bugged me;
After forcing myself to grind through the last several days (there was some good story content mixed in which helped me here). I finally got to the last class. The ultimate combination of my 40+ hours of exploration, grinding, sleuthing, helping, and discovery. The final reward, a group photo and a bump to the title screen. To be clear, the journey was fairly fun (if grandly), but the complete lack of anything resembling an epilogue was just a disappointing cherry on an ‘ok’ second half of the game.

Conclusion;
As a fan of the QFG games AND a fan of point and click games AND as someone who enjoys the Coles (Writers) storytelling style AND given that I paid $15 for the game…. With all this, it was worth it for me.
However, I highly doubt that I am in the majority. Fans of QFG will find a flawed game that provides enough enjoyment to make it work playing. Non-fans will likely enjoy the first several ‘in-game days’ before realizing that, outside of some scripted events, that’s as good as it gets.
Hero U is a mix between an annoying game of repetition and poor design, combined with a fantastic revisit to one of my favorite gaming worlds. The result is a game that I both enjoyed (at times, when something new game up) and truly felt wasted my time at others (grind stat, grind rep, grind money, revisit a location, run the hallways, check for something new). 
I have read that this is supposed to be the first in a new trilogy by the developers. On the one hand, I hope that this is true, as I would like to revisit this world. On the other hand, many of the elements that I loved about the QFG games, such as exploring new places and meeting new peoples, these elements are extremely limited in this game. You meet a half dozen classmates, and about the same number of teachers, and you are confined to the school the whole game….
QFG had me defeating brigands, making camps in the Savanna, sleeping under the protection of magical trees and saving cities from djinn, and defeating dark gods... Hero U…rat’s in the basement (there is more later)… it is just limited.. in almost every metric by comparison, both in scope and depth.
Will I play the sequel?  Probably, I just hope that they don’t stick with the Hero U ‘stuck at school’ day-to-day grind motif.

This is a decent game, although it's not quite what I expected.  I had been expecting more puzzle and adventure game elements, but this game is definitely more of an RPG.  You play as a young wannabe thief, Shawn.  Shawn is caught during his very first break-in attempt and is enrolled by a mysterious benefactor to study as a Rogue at hero school.  Rogues consider themselves to be far superior to thieves; rogues are charming and honorable and brave, and thieves are selfish cutthroats.

The game unfolds over 50 days.  You are on a strict clock, but the clock is more turn-based than real-time.  If you stand still and take no actions, time will not pass.  Time only passes when you walk or interact with any object or person. Most days unfold using the exact same schedule.  You have to be in class until 2, there is an elective at 3 that the game strongly suggests you take, you have to show up at the dining hall between 5 and 6 PM, curfew is at 10, and bedtime is around midnight.  If you go to bed after midnight, you will suffer (minor) penalties on the following day.  The game definitely railroads you onto this schedule, so if you try to pump iron in the gym instead of going to dinner, the game will warp you to the dining hall, and if you try to read a book in the library too close to curfew, Shawn will refuse to do it.  

Time comes at a premium in Hero-U, so a lot of the game is figuring out how to cram in enough activities to raise your stats.  You will spend most of your days following the same basic routine: Class, gym, elective, dinner, rec room, sneaking about a bit, bed, repeat.  It is very fun to see the stats increase at first, but by the end of the game I had most things maxed out and I did not notice very much difference in the gameplay.

There is also a social aspect in the game.  Shawn can chat with and make friends with a number of teachers and staff, his roommate, and his classmates.  The characters are all a bit flat, and friendships don't have too much of a gameplay benefit, but nonetheless I found this aspect of the game to be welcome.  There's even a bit of a romance aspect tacked on with both men and women to flirt with, which is quite minimal but also a nice touch.

Most of the aspects of Hero-U could be best described as "adequate, if not stellar".  The combat works and gets the job done.  The abundance of time-gated content is a bit frustrating, but understandable.  The character progression, world-building, and overall story is decent.  

There is one place where Hero-U really shines, though, and that is the attention to detail with with the environment and the general writing with the flavor text.  Every picture, every suit of armor, every random pot and bush and tree has multiple interaction options.  These serve zero gameplay purpose, but the writing that went into these things is enjoyable and warm and funny.  There's a staggering amount of well-written flavor text hidden away in this game which has no function other than to reward exploration.  These delightful puns and other tidbits are funny, cheerful, and somehow nostalgic.

There's a lot here to make me optimistic about Summer Daze, and I will be picking it up as soon as it is available.

‘Hero-U: Rogue to Redemption’ is a point-and-click adventure game with RPG elements, made by the creators of 'Quest for Glory' series. While trying to steal an item, our character Shawn gets caught and sent to the Hero University where young people learn to use their strengths and become heroes worthy to society. Shawn, being rather light on moral principles, is assigned to a Rogue class.

From then on, we play through each in-game day, go to the class in the morning, and after that do a variety of other things - we can build relations with our classmates and get to know them better, we can practice and improve our skills, we can go into dungeon areas to fight monsters and find loot, or we can do various quests that pop up. Over time we get to explore more of the university and learn a lot about the game's rich world and backstories of each character, as well as our own. On top of all this, there are plenty of jokes and humourous moments.

In addition to point-and-click mechanics and interactions with the environment, the game also has RPG elements such as skills that we can improve throughout the game and relationship-building with NPCs (this includes all relations, friendship and romance alike). Aside from this, there is also time management. The time does not tick down in a live manner. Rather each activity we do and each dialogue we have causes some in-game time to elapse. At specific times in a day, certain things happen, such as class, dinner, bedtime, etc.

In some of the dungeon areas we can end up engaging in combat with various creatures. The combat is turn-based and allows for some tactics to be used. It is also avoidable as our character can sneak past the enemies too with enough patience and stealth stat. 

There are also many puzzles and mini-games to do, some of which are done during our exploration of dungeons, and other times when doing other activities.

Many of our choices and actions (or inactions) have consequences and can alter how some events happen and what happens to other characters.

Overall, a really fun hybrid of RPG and point-and-click adventure, with a really strong narrative and world-building, many fun gameplay mechanics that come together very well, and a nice level of presentation with a lot of beautiful art. 

For a more in-depth review, please check here: https://saveorquit.com/2020/08/31/review-hero-u-rogue-to-redemption/

Fantastic spiritual successor to Quest for Glory series in many ways (It's set in the same universe you'll find out)     It's pretty much if you combined being a student at Hogwartz with the Quest for Glory world, but instead of learning to be a wizard, you're learning to be a rogue.

Very deep, very relatable class mates you just want to all make friends with. Well except for one.  Every university has a jerk teacher on the faculty and a "Malfoy" type right?

Possible Cons:

- The university is very regimented and you have to be at certain places at certain times.   People who don't like this type of restriction in an RPG/Adventure Game will feel cramped and not a true sense of freedom.   Often you're in the middle of something and you run out of time and the game warps you to dinner or your doorm room to go to sleep.

- The game does not explain that many major quests through the semester have a very short period of time to complete and there is often no real warning.   I used many saves and walkthrough peeks to see what had time limits.

- Combat in the later parts of the game can be very difficult if you didn't use your precious limited outside of classroom time to buff up your fighting/sneaking/defense skills.  

Totally recommend it despite the cons.  I was hooked from start to finish. Please make a sequel.

Unique and very enjoyable game! Some people have apparently been scared off by talk of objectives having a "time limit"--don't be. Time does pass during the game, but it just forces you to chose from several optional activities--raising stats and skills, exploring, studying, etc.--you do have to make some choices, but there is plenty of time to accomplish what you need to do over the 50 days allowed. Interesting story, characters, and setting. I kept coming back and played this game pretty much exclusively because I wanted to see the story unfold--took me 55 hours to complete. If you like adventure and role-playing coupled with a great story, you will enjoy this game. Recommended 9/10.
Reminiscence of the old days Quest for Glory series. Though the turn based combat and the one icon interaction needs to get use to.

I loved the Quest For Glory games as a kid so I found Hero-U to be blissfully nostalgic. It has that classic sierra point and click adventure game look and feel, it is full of references to the old QFG games, and it has that pun filled humour QFG fans know and love.

Fantastic! I wouldn't have expected that I would like this game so much. It lacks the high stakes and dark tones of the RPGs I've been playing recently, though you prowl catacombs and talk to spirits. Instead it has an atmosphere of warmth, familiarity and comfort. I could describe this game, though it has the prerequisites of exploration and derring do that an adventure game entails, as downright cozy.  It has the much fun of a puzzle game of the Lucas Arts tradition but without the frustrating blocks those games can entail. Instead you explore the castle and bond with the other students and staff at your own pace, with the main restriction being limited time due to a school schedule. The game teases you with just enough clues and allusions to keep the mysteries alluring. 
My only complaint would be the sheer volume fan insert portraits and objects and boy, there a lot of them. This game seems to have been highly crowdfunded, and while I appreciate that they helped bring the game to life, the sheer excess of them (there are more of them than actual clue containing portraits and objects) becomes confusing. It would have been helpful if they were given different color frames or other devices so the player could avoid them while searching for clues.

I've been fiddling with stuff like Academagia and Long Live The Queen to capture the bit of something that I was missing from my good ol' days of gaming. I finally picked this up and realized I was missing Hero Quest, and this has scratched that itch very well. I rarely complete games anymore as they don't hold my attention, or worse, real life catches up, but as I approach the end (I think) of this one, I'm looking forward to a replay already.

Some of the timelines are tight, but I think it's best to skip the walkthroughs and maps and just plan to replay, like we used to do before the Internet. The effort to create variety in play is enough to support that. I really feel that the rogue class is a tip of the hat to all of us who used to score over the max number of points because of the way rogues worked in the original game (back in the 80s, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥), so there's a sense that you have to complete everything and be perfect. You can, but you don't need to. Take it easy and enjoy the masterpiece and play through more than once.

The weaker points: 
 * The save system which, perhaps, is another poke at nostalgia. It's fast, it works fine, but you end up with a bazillion saves. It feels clunky and a bit hard to manage, and I'm wary of when I need to go clean house. All things considered, most people won't notice this, but it'd be nice if saves were at least grouped by playthrough, ala stellaris.
 * You can only sell one item at a time in the shop. When I have 50 dried fish to sell, that's a pain.
 * I had two fine knives (or whatever) to sell at one point, and I believe they had different selling prices. Should they have the same name, did I miss something, was there something I missed in the description? 
 * There may actually be too many puns.
 * I think having all the text voiced-over would be amazing, but given the price of the game, I can see that being tricky. I bet if they added mod support for this there'd be some enterprising folks who'd just make it happen.

I'm really trying to find things to point out that could be better, but I feel I'm scraping the bottom of the barrel. The game is really great and you should buy it. I think even not on sale it's worthwhile, but I often only buy stuff on sale so I can "justify" it to my wife :D

A solid game overall.

Some areas could stand to be standardized, some options will indicate what stat they use and some won't.  Some characters could be better explored, we barely have any interaction with your family.  And the game could definitely stand to remember your past actions better, you hear directly from an important ghost how they died so why do I keep asking people? But the basic mechanics are good and the writing and characters have sufficient charm to keep things going.

In general I'd consider it a good small scope game about learning skills and putting them to use, rather than going out and saving cities or the world.  Definitely looking forward to more.

If you want to see the best that adventure games can offer look no further. Lori & Corey Cole's commitment to releasing a quality product comes through time and again. Grateful they took six years to get it right rather than worry about profits. You won't hear about big gaming Executives taking out home equity loans to release their yearly sub-par products.  For Lori and Corey it's more about the experience for the player than it is about profits. We need more developers with their passion and dedication. Can't wait for the next one.
